description: We’re planning on building a public tool to help farmers adapt to climate shifts, starting with the coming 2026 El Niño. It will give them practical guidance so they can prepare. We are working on a real problem that affects people’s food and income.
summary:
Oscillation Nation is an interactive map that shows Canadian farmers how El Niño affects their own land. Canada is split into ecodistricts. Each one holds averaged data on temperature, precipitation, soil moisture, soil type, crops planted, crop yields, seeded area and irrigation. A timeline runs on the Oceanic Niño Index, from 1981 through the current seasonal forecast. Users can scrub through past El Niño and La Niña years and watch conditions change across the country.

The main feature is “Places like yours.” A farmer picks their ecodistrict and the tool searches every other district and years for the closest match in climate and soil. Each match comes with a similarity score and a one-click comparison report.

The challenge is that El Niño hits every farm differently, and national averages don’t tell one farmer what to expect. Oscillation Nation links a forecast to real places that have already lived through the same conditions. Farmers can see what grew there, how yields turned out and what practices held up. That lets them plan ahead with evidence instead of reacting after the season is lost.
details:
What it does: Oscillation Nation is a web map of Canada’s farmland ecodistricts. A timeline driven by the Oceanic Niño Index runs from 1981 into the current seasonal forecast. Users can scrub through El Niño and La Niña years and see climate, soil, crops, yield, seeded area, irrigation and farm payments for each district. The “Places like yours” feature takes your district and finds the most similar districts and years, each with a similarity score. Clicking a match opens a comparison report you can download as a PDF.

Benefits and impact: It turns a global climate signal into a local question: where has it already been like this, and what happened there? Farmers can choose crops, seed and irrigation ahead of the season, based on real places, instead of reacting after a loss. It’s free, needs no account and works on phones.

Tools:

  • Code: JavaScript, HTML and CSS with MapLibre GL JS and OpenFreeMap tiles.
  • Data pipeline: Python and Bash.
  • Hosting: a static site on Porkbun, with no backend.
  • Data sources: AAFC, Statistics Canada, NASA POWER, NOAA and Meteomatics (ECMWF forecast).

Creativity: Most El Niño tools try to predict the weather. Ours treats history and geography as a library of past experiments. Matches work across both place and time, so your forecast July might look most like Saskatchewan in 1998.

Factors considered:

  • Datasets come at different scales, and each layer says which one it uses.
  • Forecast data is clearly marked as forecast.
  • Districts are compared only within the same calendar month.
  • Labels are in plain language for farmers.
  • Data is precomputed so the site loads quickly on rural internet.
  • Nearly all the data is open (Open Government Licence – Canada).
